 IRS announces new 401(k) limits in 2027 for savers who hit the max
 Susan Tompor, Detroit Free Press Fri, November 13, 2026 at 7:04 AM EST 3 min read Many savers who love to stuff their retirement plans to the max will be allowed to set aside an extra $1,000 a year in their 401(k) plans in 2027 based on new contribution limits announced by the Internal Revenue Service. 
 And some savers who are 50 and older can boost their savings even more than that if they are able. 
 The baseline amount that individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans has increased to $25,500 in 2027, up from $24,500 for 2026. 
 The new limit also applies to those who participate in 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan. 
 Many Gen X savers, depending on their age, can contribute more than $25,500 next year. And a limited group of others can save even more than those 50 and older. 
 According to the IRS announcement on Thursday, Nov. 12, the catch-up contribution limit that generally applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in these plans at work is increased to $8,500 in 2027, up from $8,000 for 2026. 
 So, theoretically, we're talking about someone in that group being allowed to contribute up to $34,000 in 2027. That's up from $32,500 each year in 2026. 
 More: IRS announces inflation bump for standard deduction and more for 2027 
 A substantially higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in these plans, thanks to a change made in SECURE 2.0. 
 For 2027, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,750 instead of the $8,500 –— which means that someone in their early 60s could contribute, again theoretically, up to $37,250. 
 Here's one caveat: Higher earners making catch up contributions now must funnel that extra money into a Roth 401(k) with after tax dollars. Employees who earned more than $155,000 in 2026 generally must put their 401(k) catch-up dollars for 2027 into a Roth 401(k) account. If your plan does not offer a Roth 401(k) option, though many do, you won't be able to make catch-up contributions. 
 The average federal income tax refund hit $2,476 — up from an average of $2,169 during the initial three weeks a year ago, according to Internal Revenue Service data. It's a gain of $307 in refund cash — or 14.2% — during the first three weeks of the 2026 tax season. The IRS also announced that the limit on annual contributions to an IRA will remain at $7,500 in 2027. 
 The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over remains at $1,100 in 2027. 
 One other update worth noting: The income phase-out range for taxpayers making contributions to a Roth IRA is increased to between $158,000 and $173,000 for singles and heads of household, up from between $153,000 and $168,000 for 2026. 
 For married couples filing jointly, the IRS stated, the income phase-out range is increased to between $250,000 and $260,000, up from between $242,000 and $252,000 for 2026. 
 Story Continues The phase-out range for a married individual filing a separate return who makes contributions to a Roth IRA is not subject to an annual cost-of-living adjustment and remains between $0 and $10,000.
